Contributing to termr

Source: CONTRIBUTING.md

Welcome and scope

Thank you for helping improve termr, a reactive terminal UI framework for R. First-time contributors are welcome. Participation in official project spaces is covered by our Code of Conduct.

Ways to contribute

Report reproducible bugs, improve documentation and examples, add tests, help reproduce terminal-specific issues, or submit focused fixes. Look for good first issue and help wanted labels when choosing a task. Use Discussions for general questions, usage help, and early ideas; use Issues for bugs and concrete proposals. Report vulnerabilities privately as described in SECURITY.md.

Before starting

Search existing issues and pull requests. You may submit a PR directly for bug fixes, documentation improvements, additional or improved tests, and small internal refactoring that preserves behavior.

Discuss the following in an Issue or Discussion and agree on the direction with the maintainer before implementation:

  • New features or widgets.
  • Significant architectural changes or major changes to established behavior.
  • Breaking changes to stable APIs or significant changes to experimental APIs.
  • New dependencies, including optional dependencies.

Discussion helps avoid spending time on changes that might not be accepted. A proposal does not guarantee implementation or acceptance.

Read the README, getting started guide, repository instructions, architecture, and API stability policy, then the guide relevant to your change under docs/.

Development environment

Fork the repository, clone your fork, and create a branch from main. Use R >= 4.1; DESCRIPTION is the dependency source of truth. From R in the repository root, install any missing packages listed in Imports and testthat for local testing. Install packages from Suggests only as needed for the tests or integrations you are working on. DBI, RSQLite, jsonlite, and knitr integrations must remain optional.

For example, once those development dependencies are available:

Rscript -e "testthat::test_local('.', filter = 'button', reporter = 'summary')"

test_local() loads the source package for you. Install roxygen2 if changing R API documentation. No IDE or additional tooling is required for ordinary fixes. Interactive apps need R or Rscript in a real terminal; see the terminal guide.

Code conventions

Follow AGENTS.md and nearby code. termr uses R6, roxygen2, and testthat edition 3. Use snake_case for functions and files and UpperCamelCase for exported R6 classes. Tests belong in tests/testthat/test-*.R; runnable examples belong in inst/examples/.

Keep terminal I/O in drivers, layout separate from painting, and widget behavior in widgets and the app layer, following ARCHITECTURE.md. Keep changes focused and preserve unrelated work. Application and extension examples must use exported, documented APIs, without termr::: or internal registries. See the API inventory, NAMESPACE, and man/ for the public reference.

Testing and validation

Add or update meaningful tests and runnable examples when behavior changes. Start with affected test files; the filter matches test file names:

Rscript -e "testthat::test_local('.', filter = 'button|focus', reporter = 'summary')"

For broader changes, run the full suite using one of:

Rscript tools/dev.R test
Rscript tools/validate-dev.R

The second command explicitly enables full non-CRAN workloads and writes a summary under R’s temporary directory. See testing for workload modes, snapshots, headless tests, and platform limits. Inspect snapshot diffs before accepting updates.

For changes affecting package installation, metadata, or examples, build and check the source package. Replace the archive placeholder with the filename printed by the build:

R CMD build .
R CMD check --no-manual --as-cran termr_<version>.tar.gz

The existing R-CMD-check workflow runs package checks and extended regressions on Linux, macOS, and Windows, including R 4.1, oldrel-1, release, and devel on Linux. It also runs CRAN incoming checks with the PDF manual, optional SQL integration, Unix PTY tests, and Windows input regressions. The pkgdown workflow builds the documentation site on PRs. Separate worker and pre-RC diagnostic workflows are targeted tools, not required checks on ordinary PRs.

For terminal changes, test the relevant behavior on an available host and record the OS, terminal, and result. Consult the platform matrix and commands and SSH guide. Headless and parser tests do not certify a terminal host. You do not need to manually test every OS; CI provides cross-platform coverage. Explain unavailable checks and let the maintainer assess any remaining coverage. Documentation-only changes normally need link and formatting checks, not the full R suite.

API compatibility

docs/stability.md is the canonical classification and versioning policy, including event, command, snapshot, and deprecation contracts. Preserve backward compatibility for stable public APIs unless a breaking change has been explicitly discussed, approved, and scheduled for an appropriate release. For stable APIs, semantic versioning means:

  • PATCH: backward-compatible fixes for behavior that contradicts documentation.
  • MINOR: backward-compatible enhancements, with the documented deprecation process.
  • MAJOR: incompatible stable API changes, following the stability policy.

Experimental APIs may evolve in minor releases without a deprecation period when impractical; compatibility is not guaranteed. Significant changes still require discussion, and the stability policy’s specific contracts still apply.

Documentation and NEWS.md

Update the canonical guide and relevant examples when behavior changes. For an agreed R API change, edit roxygen comments in R/ and regenerate with:

Rscript tools/dev.R doc

Do not edit generated man/ files or NAMESPACE by hand. Avoid bare Rscript tools/dev.R when documentation regeneration is outside scope: its default mode regenerates documentation and runs tests.

Add a concise NEWS.md entry for user-visible fixes and features, experimental API changes, deprecations, and breaking changes. Include migration guidance where needed; minor editorial or internal-only changes usually do not need a NEWS entry. Coordinate release placement with the maintainer.

Pull request workflow

  1. Make a focused change on your branch and update relevant tests and docs.
  2. Review your diff and run checks appropriate to the change.
  3. Open a PR against main using the template. Explain the problem, resulting behavior, related issues or prior discussion, and compatibility impact.
  4. Record commands actually run and their results. Explain skipped or unavailable checks; leave unperformed validation unchecked.
  5. Respond to review and update the branch as needed. Draft PRs are welcome for work that is not ready for acceptance.

The standard merge strategy is Squash and merge: each accepted PR becomes one meaningful commit on main. You do not need to squash your branch manually.

Review and maintenance expectations

termr currently has one maintainer, who has final authority over architecture, public API decisions, PR acceptance, and releases. External contributions are welcome; contributing does not automatically grant merge permissions.

Review happens as maintainer capacity allows, without fixed issue or PR response times. The maintainer may request changes, defer a proposal, or decline work that does not fit the project. Small, well-explained contributions are easier to review and maintain. GitHub administrators can find the remaining repository configuration steps in Community setup.
